content.title: About
content.content: Meat or poultry‑filled pastries are baked goods made from yeast or puff pastry dough, stuffed with cooked, fried or stewed meat, poultry and sometimes vegetables. They are popular in Russia and CIS countries as a quick snack or part of a traditional meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑filled pastries appeared in Russian cuisine in the 19th century as street food.
The dough can be either yeasted or puff pastry, giving different textures.
Typical fillings include beef, pork, chicken or turkey, often with onion and spices.
During the Soviet era, large batches were produced and frozen for later reheating.
Some regions add a special meat broth to the filling to enhance flavor.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The filling supplies B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of dough and meat offers a quick source of energy, useful during physical activity.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Both the dough and meat can contain saturated fats, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Commercial products often contain added salt and preservatives, which may be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pastries can be eaten hot or warm, reheated in an oven, microwave or skillet. They are often served with mustard, sour cream or tomato sauce. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain dough version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pastries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag – they keep flavor for up to 2 months. Before eating, reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.
